explanation:
[EFFECT] Windspeed has an overall **negative** effect on predicted bike demand: at very low wind speeds (close to 0 km/h), the model assigns a small positive contribution, but as wind speed rises above that calm baseline, the contribution turns negative and falls steadily. At very high wind speeds (above roughly 33 km/h normalised ≈ 0.5), the negative impact becomes steep and severe — at the most extreme recorded speeds, the model suppresses demand by a large margin. The shape is mostly a declining curve, with a slight uptick only at the very calmest conditions.

[IMPORTANCE] Windspeed is the **second-least important** feature in the model, ranked **8th out of 9**, with an importance score of only 0.02. This is roughly 40 times smaller than the top feature (hour of the day) and about a quarter of the next-lowest feature (weather situation). In most hours, windspeed has only a minor effect on the demand forecast.

[RECOMMENDATION] Because high wind speeds meaningfully suppress predicted demand, consider reducing bike redistribution efforts and available inventory at stations during stormy or very windy periods (above ~33 km/h), while expecting near-normal demand on calm days — though since windspeed is a minor driver overall, operational decisions should primarily be guided by time-of-day and temperature patterns.
